## Overview

Every year each state reports to the Federal Highway Administration what its highway agency spent on capital projects, and what kind of work the money paid for. This project pulls those reports for 2012 to 2024 and asks three questions. How much goes to repaving and repairing the roads that already exist? What is that money worth once rising construction prices are taken out? And how many miles of road does it cover?

The spending reports do not single out resurfacing. Most states fold it into a broader line, so the spending measure is FHWA's "3R" group: resurfacing, restoration, rehabilitation, and minor widening.

## Key Findings

- **Spending rose on paper.** States spent \$35\.1 billion on 3R work in 2024, against \$18\.0 billion in 2012.
- **Prices rose faster.** Highway construction prices rose 102% over the same years. In 2024 prices, 3R spending fell 3% between 2012 and 2024, and it peaked in 2020.
- **The share held steady.** 3R work took 33% of state highway capital spending in 2024, against 27% in 2012. It is the largest single use of the money.
- **Fewer miles, and fewer miles per dollar.** Federal-aid repaving projects covered 54\,079 miles in 2012 and 31\,308 in 2024. A million dollars, in 2024 prices, covered 2\.6 miles in 2012 and 1\.9 in 2024.

## Reading the Numbers

- **Inflation adjustment.** Dollars are restated in 2024 prices using FHWA's National Highway Construction Cost Index, averaged over each calendar year.
- **Two different sets of projects.** Spending comes from what state highway agencies paid out. Miles come from projects with federal-aid funds authorized that fiscal year, and are divided only by those projects' own costs. The two charts should not be combined.
- **Miles per dollar is not only about prices.** Prices are already taken out, so a fall can also mean heavier work per mile, more urban and multi-lane roads, or more safety and drainage work inside the same project. The table counts centerline miles, not lane-miles.
- **State agencies only.** What cities and counties spend on their own streets is not in these reports.
- **Local-class roads are left out of spending.** They only appear in the table from 2015, so they are dropped to keep every year comparable.
- **Gaps and reused figures.** FHWA published no miles table in its 2021 edition. When a state does not report, FHWA carries its previous year's numbers forward.

## Data and Code

The sources are FHWA Highway Statistics Tables SF-12A and FA-10, one workbook per year, and FHWA's National Highway Construction Cost Index. The [data notebook](road-paving.ipynb) downloads them, reads every sheet, and checks each column against the totals FHWA publishes before any figure is used.

The code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/eschnitger/eschnitger.github.io/tree/main/projects/road-paving).
